response.text:
Published evidence supports context use, but does not establish that adaptive multi-scale pooling beats a five-item residual. [SASRec](https://arxiv.org/html/1808.09781) reports worse performance with zero attention blocks—the last-item-only variant—and broader attention on dense datasets. However, attention plots do not isolate learned scale selection. [Residual Dominance (RecSys 2026)](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.14021v1) provides stronger diagnostics: shuffling earlier items while preserving the last item changes predictions much less than full shuffling; residual pathways preserve same-position information despite contextual attention. Reducing residual strength recovers some misses but lowers overall accuracy. More contextual mixing therefore does not automatically improve recommendation.

Repetition and norms are separate confounds. [RepeatNet](https://staff.fnwi.uva.nl/m.derijke/wp-content/papercite-data/pdf/ren-repeatnet-2019.pdf) separates repeat/non-repeat targets: improvements mainly come from repeated consumption, with some degradation on non-repeat sessions. [Repetition and Exploration](https://staff.fnwi.uva.nl/m.derijke/wp-content/papercite-data/pdf/li-2023-repetition.pdf) further identifies repetitive bias and sensitivity to shared input/output embeddings. [NISER](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.04276) links popularity bias partly to embedding magnitudes and improves long-tail recommendation through normalization; this is session-based evidence, not direct proof for SASRec pooling.

Recommended controls, inferred from these findings: compare identical backbones with no added residual, last-item residual, fixed five-item mean, fixed multi-window mixture, global learned mixture, and context-dependent gates. Match tuning effort and normalize branch magnitudes. Preserve the last item while perturbing earlier context; separately measure sensitivity to repeated history entries without changing official splits. Report validation gains by history length, repetition, and training-item popularity; compare dot-product versus normalized scoring. Keep pinned macro HR@10 as the selection metric. Adaptive scale selection is supported only if it consistently beats fixed mixtures and five-item pooling after these controls.
